items.title: First-mover advantage is more often a myth than a rule
items.claim: Gerard Tellis and Peter Golder studied first movers across 50 product categories. What did they find?

options.text: First movers won permanently in nearly all categories
About 47% of first movers failed and the average market share of survivors was around 10%; long-term winners were more often early followers than pioneers

items.reveal:
Tellis and Golder's 'Will and Vision' (2002) and earlier paper analysed product categories from photocopiers to disposable nappies. Pioneers identified: Chux nappies (replaced by Pampers); WordStar (overtaken by Word); Friendster and MySpace (overtaken by Facebook); AltaVista (overtaken by Google).

Later entrants benefit from market education done by pioneers, technology improvements, and clearer customer preferences. The 'first mover advantage' framing oversells a narrow set of cases (network-effect platforms) as if it were general.
items.why: Business teaching often treats first-mover advantage as a strategic prize. Empirical work suggests being the right mover at the right time is more important than being first.

items.title: Maslow's pyramid was never drawn by Maslow
items.claim: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs is taught with a pyramid. What did Maslow himself draw?

options.text: He drew the pyramid himself in his 1943 paper
He never drew it as a pyramid; the pyramid representation was introduced by management consultants and textbooks in the 1960s
He drew it as a circle to indicate non-linear progression
He explicitly rejected any visual representation

items.reveal:
Todd Bridgman, Stephen Cummings and John Ballard's 2019 paper in the Academy of Management Learning & Education traced the pyramid to Charles McDermid's 1960 management article in Business Horizons. Maslow's 1943 'A Theory of Human Motivation' described needs as overlapping and dynamic — not rigidly tiered.

Maslow himself, late in his career, qualified the theory heavily: needs can be pursued in parallel, prioritisation varies by culture and individual, and self-actualisation isn't a 'top' level so much as a developmental orientation.

Empirical tests find weak support for the strict hierarchy.
items.why: The most-taught motivation diagram in business education was drawn by someone other than the named theorist and oversimplifies what he wrote. Worth checking what's in the textbook against what's in the source.

items.title: The Hawthorne effect is real but smaller than the textbook story
items.claim: Elton Mayo's Hawthorne studies (1927-32) are taught as showing that worker productivity rose because of attention paid to them. What does re-analysis of the original data show?

options.text: The effect was even larger than originally reported

Levitt and List's 2011 re-analysis of original records suggests the 'Hawthorne effect' was much weaker than reported; productivity gains were largely explained by which workers were replaced and the Monday rebound after weekends
No data from the studies survived
The lighting reduction was actually the cause

items.reveal:
Steven Levitt and John List (American Economic Journal, 2011) accessed original Hawthorne Works data digitised by the University of Wisconsin. They found the famous 'productivity rose whatever you changed' pattern was much weaker than Mayo claimed and largely artifactual.

The broader 'human relations' school it spawned remained influential — but the founding evidence base was weaker than generations of textbooks suggested.
items.why: Iconic findings get retold long after the evidence has been challenged. Modern HR theory survives, but its founding study should be taught with caveats.
